title: How Curiosity Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how curiosity works. They open with the origin of the proverb "curiosity killed the cat" (traced to Ben Johnson's play Every Man in His Humour, and first in print in the Galveston Daily News as "Thomas cat"), then discuss why curiosity persists evolutionarily despite risk. They cover the two rival theories, drive theory and incongruity theory, and the state versus trait curiosity distinction, with trait split into depth and breadth. They cover the historical suspicion of curiosity in the Middle Ages (Saint Augustine), curiosity and aging and Alzheimer's, curiosity and attraction between people, the dopamine reward system and the D4 dopamine receptor gene in curious great tit songbirds, and the dentate gyrus in the hippocampus. Sensory-deprivation and animal exploration experiments are mentioned. The episode ends with listener mail about World Bicycle Relief and a call for listener questions.
topics: origin of proverb curiosity killed the cat
Ben Johnson Every Man in His Humour

segments.title: Opening banter and WFMU radio plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck plug their WFMU radio airing and Chuck's upcoming trip to Maximum Fun Con, then Josh introduces the topic of the cat proverb.

segments.title: Origin of 'curiosity killed the cat'
segments.summary: Josh traces the proverb to Ben Johnson's play Every Man in His Humour, where a line mentions care killing a cat, and to its first print appearance in the Galveston Daily News as 'Thomas cat'. He also mentions the Discovery curiosity.com project he was asked to write about.
topics: Ben Johnson Every Man in His Humour

segments.title: Curiosity and evolution
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss how curiosity seems to conflict with survival, using a caveman example, and argue that curiosity still supports survival by finding food, and that it is the opposite of fear. They note that many advances like penicillin came from curiosity.

segments.title: Drive theory versus incongruity theory
segments.summary: The hosts explain the two rival theories: drive theory, an internal hunger for superfluous information, and incongruity theory, a response to external stimuli that break expected order. They note each has a hole that the other can fill.

segments.title: State and trait curiosity, depth and breadth
segments.summary: They distinguish state curiosity, which is situational and fleeting, from trait curiosity, a lifelong disposition, citing Ernest Becker and death. Trait curiosity is further split into depth and breadth, and they discuss the value of each in colleges.

segments.title: Curiosity's history, aging, and development
segments.summary: They discuss Saint Augustine's condemnation of curiosity in the Middle Ages, the link between low curiosity and Alzheimer's patients, and the way curiosity starts in infancy and is shaped by experience. Sensory-deprivation experiments of the 1950s and 1960s and animal exploration studies are mentioned.

segments.title: Curiosity, identity, and attraction
segments.summary: They discuss how curiosity shapes identity and why curious people are attracted to other curious people, citing a 2004 University of Texas study on trait curiosity and attraction.

segments.title: Dopamine, the D4 gene, and the brain
segments.summary: They describe the D4 dopamine gene linked to curiosity in great tit songbirds, the role of dopamine as a reward, and the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus as a curiosity region that helps distinguish novel from familiar situations.

segments.title: Personal anecdote on curiosity and fear
segments.summary: Chuck describes himself as curious with a balance of fear and curiosity, and the hosts close the theory discussion.

segments.title: Listener mail: World Bicycle Relief
segments.summary: A listener named Kristen describes her work for World Bicycle Relief in Zambia, which builds and distributes bicycles to students, especially girls, to improve school attendance. The hosts then ask for listener questions and podcast ideas.

segments.title: Sign-off and promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote the Stuff from the Future video podcast and sign off.
